lessons.title: Why fruit trees need fertiliser
lessons.html:
Food for the trees

Deciduous fruit trees, such as apples, pears, peaches, plums, nectarines and apricots, lose their leaves in winter. In the Western Cape and other fruit areas, these trees grow new leaves, flowers and fruit every year. To do this they need food from the soil. This food is called nutrients. When the soil does not have enough nutrients, we add fertiliser.

The main nutrients

NutrientWhat it doesSign it is short
Nitrogen (N)Green leaves and growthPale yellow-green leaves, weak growth
Phosphorus (P)Roots and flowersPoor root growth, dull leaves
Potassium (K)Fruit size, colour and qualityBrown, burnt leaf edges, small fruit
Calcium (Ca)Firm fruit that stores wellSpots on apples such as bitter pit

Who decides how much?

The farm manager or adviser decides which fertiliser to use, how much and when. They use soil tests and leaf tests to see what the trees need. Your job is to apply the fertiliser exactly as you are told. Too little and the trees grow poorly. Too much wastes money, can burn roots and can wash into rivers and dams.

When fertiliser is applied

Fertiliser is usually given at certain times of the year, for example in spring when growth starts and after harvest. Your supervisor will give you the programme for each block. Never change the amounts on your own.

Types of fertiliser

  • Granules spread by hand or with a spreader on the soil.
  • Liquid fertiliser given through the irrigation (fertigation).
  • Foliar sprays sprayed on the leaves.
  • Organic fertiliser such as compost or manure.

lessons.title: Applying fertiliser in the orchard
lessons.html:
Before you start

  1. Get your instructions: which block, which fertiliser, how much per tree or per row.
  2. Put on your PPE: gloves, overall, closed shoes and a dust mask if the product is dusty. Read or ask about the label.
  3. Collect the fertiliser from the store and check the name on the bag matches your instructions.
  4. Get the correct measuring container, for example a marked cup or tin, so every tree gets the same amount.

Spreading by hand

  • Measure the amount for one tree.
  • Spread it evenly in a band on the soil under the outer part of the tree canopy, where the feeding roots are. This is called the drip line.
  • Do not pile fertiliser against the trunk. It can burn the bark and roots.
  • Keep fertiliser out of irrigation furrows and away from dams and rivers.
  • Do not apply on very windy days or just before heavy rain.

After applying

Often the block is irrigated after spreading so the fertiliser moves into the soil. Follow your supervisor's instruction on this.

Records

Write down the date, block number, fertiliser name, amount used and your name. The farm needs these records for its programme and for export rules.

Safety and storage

  • Wash your hands before eating, drinking or smoking.
  • Store fertiliser in a dry, locked store, off the floor, away from food and animal feed.
  • Close bags properly. Sweep up spills and do not wash them into drains.
  • Some fertilisers can burn or catch fire when mixed with fuel. Never store fertiliser with diesel or oil.

If fertiliser gets in your eyes, rinse with lots of clean water and tell your supervisor.

Key points

  • Fruit trees need nutrients such as N, P, K and calcium.
  • The manager decides type and amount from soil and leaf tests.
  • Measure carefully and spread evenly under the outer canopy, not against the trunk.
  • Wear PPE and wash your hands after work.
  • Record what you applied, where and when.
